rationale.conceptual: The method involves spin-polarized DFT, harmonic vibrational analysis, and the computational hydrogen electrode (CHE) model. While these are standard techniques in computational catalysis, correctly applying them requires understanding of convergence, reference states, and free-energy corrections, making it a careful, non-trivial implementation.
rationale.execution: The workflow consists of two preliminary geometry relaxations (pristine g-C₃N₄ and Cu@g-C₃N₄) followed by energy calculations for at least 16 different adsorbate/gas‑phase configurations, each potentially requiring separate DFT runs with vibrational analysis. This multi-stage pipeline with fragile tooling (Quantum ESPRESSO input generation, job management, post-processing) and many load‑bearing handoffs drives a high execution complexity.

difficulty.reasoning: The task requires reproducing standard DFT free-energy diagrams using the CHE model, which involves multiple geometry optimizations and single-point calculations. The method is well-established, so conceptual difficulty is moderate. The pipeline is long with many dependencies (∼20 DFT jobs plus post-processing), making execution more challenging. Resource-wise, it is a CPU-bound DFT workflow on a moderate-sized slab (∼100 atoms), so no GPU needed, modest RAM.
